searches.note: Twenty six searches of a share of twenty eight, two left unspent, none of them the author's. Three were shared across the group: the Swartland Revolution twice (its founders, its first edition and its end, once open and once restricted to winemag, The Wine Society, Jancis Robinson and Decanter) and the Swartland Independent Producers. Four were restricted to a house's own domain (Sadie's sheets, Mullineux and Leeu's sheets, AA Badenhorst's pages, Allesverloren's pages); the others kept the house's domain out where the author had leant on it, so that each second source would be independent. One search on Columella's soils returned nothing of the house. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail stood in no source read, or in one page that is not the house speaking of itself, it was cut or said with less; the house's own claims are told as its account.

Writers' own sites met among the results (Wine with Seth, Wine Anorak, a Master of Wine's blog, a critic's site) are cited neither in the fragment nor here. Pages whose addresses name a living person (winemag columns under a writer's name, the Swartland route's interview with the Allesverloren family, a Vinous piece whose address names a living winemaker) are cited here by their bare addresses or not at all.
The serving temperatures follow the Codex's service reference: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius for the three dry reds and the Cape Vintage, 10 to 13 for the full white; no air is promised to soften tannin.
The two renames were tested in memory: the plan with each new wine and the records with the edits set out below lint with no problem.

tested: The founding of 1999 and the first Columella of 2000: Wikipedia and two merchants with the house's domain kept out; the library's year stands. Sound.
The founder at Spice Route: 1997 or 1998 by account, the first vintages made in its cellar. Changed to the late 1990s.

The making: open 3,300 litre concrete, a natural ferment of about three weeks at 24 degrees and about three weeks more on the skins, basket press, malolactic in barrel, a year in French oak with 5 to 10 per cent new, a year in large oval foudres, unfined and unfiltered: the house's sheets of 2013 to 2024, Broadbent, Gourmet Hunters and Cavesa. Sound.

The grapes: Pinotage in recent vintages by the 2024 sheet and Wikipedia; the first vintage almost all Syrah stands against Wikipedia's Syrah, Mourvèdre and Grenache, so the story no longer orders the grapes after it. Changed.

The sites: Paardeberg, Kasteelberg, Malmesbury and Piquetberg by the sheets and merchants; the soils named by the author were in no source; one search on the soils returned nothing of the house. Changed.

The Swartland Revolution: founded in 2010 by the four houses, first held at Riebeek-Kasteel in November 2010, discontinued after 2015 (The Wine Society, winemag); a reunion was held in 2025, which the stories need not tell. The Swartland Independent Producers formed in 2011 (Farmers Weekly, winemag). Sound, with the place of later editions softened.

The label: Columella and Palladius as Roman writers on farming (Wikipedia, the Oxford Companion to Wine as the author read it). Wine of Origin Swartland: one secondary only, so left open. The house calls the grapes Mediterranean red varieties in its general introduction, so the table's word stands.
Cards and questions: one right answer each, distractors of one kind, the explanations teach. Rules: nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, British, no dash. Sound.

changed.was: The founder had worked as a winemaker at Spice Route in the Swartland from 1998, and in 1999 he set up the family's own company, whose early wines were made in Spice Route's cellar. Columella was first made with the 2000 vintage, almost all Syrah from old bush vines. From that first year the house resolved to keep its policies in vineyard and cellar for at least ten years before judging them. Mourvèdre soon joined the Syrah, then Grenache, and later Carignan, Cinsaut and Tinta Barocca, as the house came to blend vineyards rather than grapes; Palladius, the white, became its counterpart, and an Old Vine Series later gathered single old parcels from across the Cape. In November 2010 the house was one of the four founders of the Swartland Revolution, a festival held at Riebeek-Kasteel each year until 2015 that drew the wine trade to a district long known for wheat and bulk wine, and in 2011 a group of the district's growers formed the Swartland Independent Producers. Looking back over twenty vintages in 2020, the house resolved to use fewer whole bunches. Columella is the wine that first showed what the old vines of the Swartland could give, and a sommelier pours it as the start of that story.
changed.now: The founder worked as a winemaker at Spice Route in the Swartland in the late 1990s, and in 1999 he set up the family's own company, whose first wines were made at Spice Route. Columella was first made with the 2000 vintage, almost all Syrah from old bush vines, and by the house's own account it resolved that year to keep its policies in vineyard and cellar for at least ten years before judging them. Over the years the share of Syrah fell as Mourvèdre and Grenache took a larger part and Carignan, Cinsaut, Tinta Barocca and lately Pinotage joined, for the house came to blend vineyards rather than grapes; Palladius, the white, became its counterpart, and an Old Vine Series later gathered single old parcels from across the Cape. In November 2010 the house was one of the four founders of the Swartland Revolution, a festival first held at Riebeek-Kasteel that ran each year until 2015 and drew the wine trade to a district long known for wheat and bulk wine, and in 2011 a group of the district's growers formed the Swartland Independent Producers. In its own review of twenty vintages, in 2020, the house resolved to use fewer whole bunches. Columella is the wine that first showed what the old vines of the Swartland could give, and a sommelier pours it as the start of that story.
changed.why: The founder's start at Spice Route is 1997 or 1998 by account, so the late 1990s. Wikipedia says the first Columella held Syrah, Mourvèdre and Grenache, others say almost all Syrah, so the story no longer says Mourvèdre joined after the first vintage; Pinotage joins lately by the 2024 sheet and Wikipedia. The ten year policy and the review of 2020 are the house's own account and now say so. The first Swartland Revolution was held at Riebeek-Kasteel in November 2010 and the festival ran to 2015; the sources read do not place every edition there. Three words were trimmed for the cap.

changed.was: The house was founded in 2007 by a winemaking couple who settled at Riebeek-Kasteel in the Swartland. Their first Syrah, of the 2008 vintage, was made at Reyneke in Stellenbosch, where they were then making wine. In November 2010 they were among the four founders of the Swartland Revolution, a festival held at Riebeek-Kasteel each year until 2015 that brought buyers and writers to a district long known for bulk wine. The same 2010 vintage began their single soil range: Syrah from schist and Syrah from granite, bottled apart so that the soils could be read side by side. The Schist parcel lies on Roundstone, the farm on the slopes of the Kasteelberg that became their home. In 2013 the couple took a partner, and the business became Mullineux and Leeu Family Wines, with a second cellar, Leeu Passant, in Franschhoek. A Syrah from iron rich soil later joined the range, beside Chenin Blanc from quartz, and the Syrahs make the case that Syrah, not Pinotage, is the Swartland's red. For a sommelier the Schist is the district's geology in a glass: one grape, one way of making, and a soil that names the bottle.

changed.was: The house was founded by two cousins of a Constantia family whose grandfather managed the farm at Groot Constantia for decades. One of them made wine at Rustenberg in Stellenbosch before, in 2008, the two bought Kalmoesfontein, an old farm on the Paardeberg in the Swartland. The farm's cellar had last made wine in the 1930s and stood neglected, and the cousins began, by the house's account, by restoring it and planting new vines beside the old bush vines already there, many of them planted in the 1950s and 1960s. The farm's buildings run back further: the Koringhuis, the old grain store, dates by the house's account to the late eighteenth century. In November 2010 the house was one of the four founders of the Swartland Revolution, the festival held at Riebeek-Kasteel each year until 2015 that drew the wine trade to the district. Its white blend was long sold as the Family White, and it later took the farm's name, Kalmoesfontein, while some merchants kept the old one. Its grapes, from small parcels across the farm, are picked on one day and fermented together, so the wine is a field blend made as one. For a sommelier it is the Swartland white blend in its plainest form: many grapes, one farm, one ferment.

changed.why: Whole bunches have been used from the start but not always entirely: 85 per cent whole bunch in 2023. About twelve months, 85 to 95 per cent in large foudres (of 2,500 litres in 2023) and the rest in concrete eggs.

changed.was: Porseleinberg, porcelain mountain in Afrikaans, is a farm on a rugged schist ridge near Riebeek-Kasteel in the Swartland. In 2009 Boekenhoutskloof, the Franschhoek house, bought it, by its own account to secure a reliable source of quality grapes, Syrah above all. The first wine came with the 2010 vintage, and the farm has made one wine ever since: a Syrah under the farm's own name. That November Porseleinberg was among the four founders of the Swartland Revolution, the festival at Riebeek-Kasteel that ran each year until 2015 and drew buyers and writers to a district long known for bulk wine. The vineyard is decomposed mica schist on hard, rocky bedrock, and the wine is made to show it: whole bunches, large foudres and concrete rather than small new barrels. The label is printed by hand on a vintage Heidelberg letterpress in the farm's own cellar. The Franschhoek house's own Syrah draws on the same vineyard, with fruit from a second site beside it, but Porseleinberg bottles the ridge alone. For a sommelier it is the Swartland's schist told through one grape on one farm.

The label is printed by hand on a vintage Heidelberg letterpress in the farm's own cellar. The Franschhoek house's own Syrah draws largely on the same vineyard, with fruit from Goldmine, a second Swartland farm, but Porseleinberg bottles the ridge alone. For a sommelier it is the Swartland's schist told through one grape on one farm.

changed.was: The estate's own history places its beginning between 1696 and 1704, when, as the house tells it, the governor of the Cape left the land to a widow named Cloete. The story goes that in 1704 the family came home from a journey to Stellenbosch to find the house burnt and the farm in ruins, and the farm took its name, Allesverloren, all is lost. In 1872 the Malan family took over the farm, and on 22 May 1874 Daniel François Malan (1874 to 1959) was born there; he became prime minister of South Africa from 1948 to 1954, and his government brought in apartheid. By the family's own account a Malan of the farm first made the fortified wine that grew into its flagship, and the family were pioneers in bringing Portuguese grapes to South Africa. The wine was sold for years as Fine Old Vintage, once with the word port beside it; South Africa later gave up the Portuguese name under an agreement with the European Union, and from the 2020 vintage the estate has called the wine Cape Vintage. Beside it the estate kept Tinta Barocca and Shiraz as dry table wines. To a sommelier it is the Swartland's older fortified tradition, made from the grapes of port, beside the district's newer dry reds.
changed.now: The estate's own history places its beginning between 1696 and 1704, when, as the house tells it, the governor of the Cape left the land to a widow named Cloete. The story goes that in 1704 the family came home from a journey to Stellenbosch to find the house burnt and the farm in ruins, and the farm took its name, Allesverloren, all is lost. In 1872 the Malan family took over the farm, and on 22 May 1874 Daniel François Malan (1874 to 1959) was born there; he became prime minister of South Africa from 1948 to 1954, and his government brought in apartheid. By the family's own account a Malan of the farm first made the fortified wine that grew into its flagship, and the family were pioneers in bringing Portuguese grapes to South Africa. The wine was long sold as Allesverloren Port. Under a wine agreement signed with the European Union in 2002, South Africa gave up the Portuguese name; the estate's wine became Fine Old Vintage, and from the 2020 vintage it has been called Cape Vintage. Beside it the estate kept Tinta Barocca and Shiraz as dry table wines. To a sommelier it is the Swartland's older fortified tradition, made from the grapes of port, beside the district's newer dry reds.
changed.why: The order of the names: wine.co.za reports the estate's Port renamed Fine Old Vintage after the European rules, Wine-Searcher files older vintages as Port, and the press release of 2024 gives Cape Vintage from the 2020 vintage. The agreement was struck in January 2002 at Nederburg, with port and sherry to go from export labels within five years and from home labels within twelve. The record had said Fine Old Vintage once carried the word port beside it, which nothing read says.
